c.tagline: Caribbean blue with Maya ruins next door.

avoid.reason: Hotel Zone safe; caution downtown (Centro) at night; cartel-related violence has risen — avoid buying drugs

hood_desc: The long barrier-island strip of high-rise beach resorts, turquoise Caribbean water, nightclubs and shopping malls. Ideal for travelers wanting all-inclusive resorts, beaches and party nightlife in one convenient stretch.

The real working city away from the beaches, with local markets, authentic taquerias, and more affordable hotels and food. Best for budget travelers and those wanting a genuine Mexican urban experience.

An upscale marina and residential development with luxury condos, a golf course, yachts, boutiques and polished restaurants. Suits visitors seeking a refined, modern base with dining and a marina setting.

A low-key port area on the north side, the departure point for ferries to Isla Mujeres, with simple local eateries and a laid-back feel. Good for travelers wanting island access and a quieter, authentic vibe.
lodging: Four Points by Sheraton Cancun Centro
Dreams Vista Cancún Golf & Spa Resort

water.note: Avoid tap water; use bottled or purified water, though hotel-made ice is usually safe.

transit.pay: Pay cash in pesos directly to the driver - the R-1 bus along the Hotel Zone costs about MX$12 (~$0.65) flat fare, and colectivo vans cost MX$10-15 (~$0.55-0.80) depending on distance. No transit card exists; exact change helps.
transit.hours: R-1 buses run about 5am-midnight along the Hotel Zone at frequent intervals; colectivos generally operate 5am-11pm with sparse late-night options via taxi.
transit.note: Most tourists use the R-1 city bus or shared colectivo vans along the Hotel Zone and to downtown; ADO runs airport/intercity buses, and taxis or ride-hailing apps cover the rest.

food.name: Cochinita pibil
food.desc: Yucatan's signature pork, marinated in achiote and sour orange, wrapped in banana leaf and slow-roasted until it shreds. Sundays are cochinita day.

places.name: El Pibito
places.note: Home-style Yucatecan cooking loved by locals; cochinita, panuchos and salbutes at low prices.

places.name: Taqueria Los 3 Reyes
places.note: Cochinita is the house specialty, served from early morning until it sells out. Go before noon.

places.name: Mercado 23
places.note: Old-school market fondas serving cochinita tacos and tortas to market workers since dawn.

food.name: Panuchos and salbutes
food.desc: Fried corn tortillas topped with turkey or cochinita, pickled red onion and habanero. Panuchos are stuffed with refried beans, salbutes are puffy.

places.name: Loncheria El Pocito
places.note: Hidden-gem lonchería known for panuchos de cochinita and very authentic Yucatecan plates.

places.name: Labna
places.note: Long-running Yucatecan restaurant near the park; a reliable sit-down intro to the regional classics.

places.name: Parque de las Palapas food stalls
places.note: Evening stalls in Cancun's main square where families eat panuchos and salbutes nightly.

food.name: Sopa de lima
food.desc: Clear turkey or chicken broth sharpened with Yucatecan lima citrus and piled with crisp tortilla strips. Served piping hot at almost every traditional table.

places.name: Labna
places.note: Classic Yucatecan menu where sopa de lima is a staple alternative to the tourist-zone restaurants.

places.name: La Habichuela
places.note: Cancun institution since 1977 blending Maya and Caribbean cooking in a garden courtyard.

places.name: Mercado 28
places.note: Market fondas ladle out sopa de lima alongside tamales and other Yucatecan home cooking.

food.name: Poc chuc
food.desc: Thin pork steaks bathed in sour orange, grilled over charcoal and served with pickled onion, black beans and grilled spring onion.

places.name: Labna
places.note: One of downtown's best-known Yucatecan kitchens; poc chuc is a menu cornerstone.

places.name: La Parrilla
places.note: Busy downtown grill on the main restaurant strip, good for regional grilled meats and mariachi.

places.name: El Pibito
places.note: Fast, cheap and genuinely Yucatecan; a favourite of locals who work downtown.

food.name: Fish tacos and ceviche
food.desc: Caribbean catch served raw in lime-cured ceviche or battered and fried into tacos, dressed with cabbage, chipotle mayo and hot sauce.

places.name: Los de Pescado
places.note: Cult local taqueria for battered fish and shrimp tacos plus ceviche tostadas; cash-friendly.

places.name: El Fish Fritanga
places.note: Lagoon-side seafood shack popular with residents; fresh ceviche with sunset water views.

places.name: Mercado 28
places.note: Seafood counters inside the market serve ceviche and cocteles at market prices.

food.name: Marquesitas
food.desc: Yucatecan street dessert: a crepe batter crisped in a waffle iron, spread with Nutella, cajeta or jam, then rolled up with grated Edam bola cheese.

places.name: Parque de las Palapas carts
places.note: The classic after-dinner ritual; carts fire up around the plaza every evening.

places.name: Mercado 23
places.note: Neighbourhood market where marquesita vendors set up alongside the food stalls at night.

places.name: Mercado 28
places.note: Marquesitas and tamales among the food stalls in Cancun's best-known market.

food.name: Xtabentun
food.desc: Maya anise-and-honey liqueur made from fermented honey of bees that feed on the xtabentun flower. Sipped neat, over ice or splashed into coffee.

places.name: La Habichuela
places.note: Maya-influenced restaurant that pours xtabentun as a digestif in its candlelit garden.

places.name: La Parrilla
places.note: Downtown restaurant with a deep Mexican spirits list including regional Yucatecan liqueurs.

places.name: Mercado 28
places.note: Market stalls sell bottled xtabentun to take home, usually cheaper than the hotel zone.

food.name: Aguas frescas and agua de chaya
food.desc: Fruit waters poured from glass jars: horchata, jamaica, tamarindo and the local green agua de chaya, made from the Yucatan's spinach-like leaf.

places.name: Mercado 23
places.note: Market juice counters blend chaya, horchata and seasonal fruit waters to order.

places.name: Mercado 28
places.note: Big jars of aguas frescas at every fonda; the cheapest way to cool down downtown.

places.name: Parque de las Palapas food stalls
places.note: Evening stands pair horchata and jamaica with panuchos and marquesitas.

landmarks: Tulum Ruins
Ancient Maya walled city perched dramatically on a cliff above turquoise Caribbean water, a rare combo of ruins and beach in one frame.
Playa Delfines
Cancún's iconic public beach with the giant 'CANCÚN' letters sign and sweeping Hotel Zone coastline views.
Cobá (Nohoch Mul Pyramid)
The tallest climbable Maya pyramid in the Yucatán, rising above dense jungle for a striking, less-crowded photo op.
Xcaret Park
Eco-archaeological park whose colorful entrance sign and underground rivers make it a favorite family and nature photo spot.
Cenote Ik Kil
A near-perfectly circular sinkhole with hanging vines and a turquoise pool 26 meters below ground, one of the region's most photogenic natural wonders.
Cancún Hotel Zone (Zona Hotelera)
A narrow barrier island lined with resort towers between the Caribbean Sea and Nichupté Lagoon, iconic for aerial and skyline shots.
El Rey Archaeological Site
Small Maya ruins right within the Hotel Zone, notable for resident iguanas posing amid ancient stone platforms.
Xel-Há Park
A natural lagoon-and-inlet eco-park with clear waters meeting the jungle, popular for snorkeling and jungle-meets-sea photography.
Museo Maya de Cancún
A modern museum in the Hotel Zone holding over 3,500 Maya artifacts, with a jungle path behind it leading to the ruined temples of San Miguelito.
La Isla Shopping Village
An open-air canal-front mall in the Hotel Zone with boutique shops, waterfront restaurants, a Ferris wheel and an aquarium along Nichupté Lagoon.

train.note: Mexico has no international passenger trains. The Tren Maya loops the Yucatán peninsula from Cancún Aeropuerto station to Playa del Carmen, Tulum, Mérida and on to Palenque — buy tickets on the official site or at the station.

bus.note: ADO's overnight coach to Belize City leaves from the downtown Cancún terminal via Playa del Carmen and Chetumal — bring your passport for the middle-of-the-night border stop and cash for Belize border fees. ADO and its sister brands also cover most Mexican long-distance routes.

ferry.note: No international ferries call at Cancún. Local Ultramar boats shuttle constantly to Isla Mujeres from Puerto Juárez, and to Cozumel from Playa del Carmen down the coast.

half.name: Tulum
half.blurb: Cliffside Maya ruins overlooking a turquoise Caribbean beach and swaying palms.

half.name: Isla Mujeres
half.blurb: Laid-back island reached by ferry, ringed by white sand and clear snorkeling waters.

half.name: Valladolid
half.blurb: Colorful colonial town of pastel facades, cenotes and relaxed Yucatecan charm.

half.name: Cozumel
half.blurb: Caribbean island famed for world-class coral reef diving and snorkeling adventures.

half.name: Playa del Carmen
half.blurb: Lively beach town with a buzzing pedestrian avenue and long stretches of sand.

full.name: Chichén Itzá
full.blurb: Wonder-of-the-world Maya city crowned by the towering El Castillo step pyramid.

Rooftop pool bar atop Nomads Hotel, downtown's easiest place to meet people
